topics.title: Enzymes: how they work
topics.intro: Enzymes are biological catalysts: proteins that speed up reactions without being used up. Each has an active site with a precise shape, so it only fits its own substrate: the lock-and-key model.
topics.teach: Explain, using the lock-and-key model, why an enzyme stops working at high temperature.
topics.talk: Ask {him} why fresh pineapple stops jelly setting (an enzyme breaks down the protein), but tinned pineapple does not.

topics.title: The heart and circulation
topics.intro: The heart is two pumps side by side: the right side sends blood to the lungs, the left side to the rest of the body. Arteries, veins and capillaries each have a structure that fits their job.
topics.teach: Explain why the left ventricle has a thicker wall than the right.
topics.talk: Take each other’s pulse before and after running up the stairs.

topics.title: Nerves, reflexes and reaction times
topics.intro: Receptors detect a stimulus; electrical impulses travel along neurones to the brain or spinal cord; effectors (muscles and glands) respond. Reflexes skip the thinking part of the brain to protect you.
topics.teach: Explain the path of a reflex arc when you touch a hot pan.
topics.talk: Try the ruler-drop test with {her}, then try it while chatting.

topics.title: Plant transport and stomata
topics.intro: Water travels up from the roots through xylem and evaporates from the leaves through stomata: transpiration. Sugars made in the leaves travel through phloem to where they are needed.
topics.teach: Explain why a plant wilts on a hot, windy day.
topics.talk: Stand a white carnation or a celery stick in coloured water and watch the xylem.

topics.title: Microbes, immunity and vaccines
topics.intro: White blood cells defend the body: some engulf pathogens, others make antibodies that lock onto them. Vaccines train the immune system in advance, so it responds faster the next time.
topics.teach: Explain why a vaccinated person usually does not become ill when they meet the real pathogen.
topics.talk: Ask {him} why antibiotics don’t work on a cold.

topics.title: Diet, food tests and energy
topics.intro: A balanced diet has carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals, fibre and water. Simple chemical tests show which nutrients a food contains.
topics.teach: Explain which test you would use to show a food contains protein, and the colour change.
topics.talk: Read a food label together and compare the energy per 100 g of two snacks.

topics.title: Classification and biodiversity
topics.intro: Linnaeus sorted living things into a hierarchy, from kingdom down to species, and gave each species a two-part Latin name. Biodiversity is the variety of life in an area, and it is under pressure from human activity.
topics.teach: Explain why biodiversity matters, with two reasons.
topics.talk: Ask {him} what Homo sapiens means (“wise human”).

topics.title: Genetic engineering and its ethics
topics.intro: Genetic engineering moves a gene from one organism into another, so it makes something new: bacteria that make human insulin, crops that resist pests. It raises big questions about safety and fairness.
topics.teach: Explain one benefit and one concern about GM crops.
topics.talk: Discuss with {him}: should we bring back extinct animals if we could?

topics.title: Formulae, equations and conservation of mass
topics.intro: A formula tells you which atoms are in a substance and how many. Because atoms are only rearranged in a reaction, the total mass stays the same, though a gas escaping can make it look as if mass is lost.
topics.teach: Explain why the mass of magnesium goes UP when it burns.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to count the atoms in H₂SO₄.

topics.title: Reactivity and extracting metals
topics.intro: How a metal is extracted depends on its reactivity. Metals below carbon in the reactivity series can be extracted by heating their ores with carbon; more reactive metals need electrolysis.
topics.teach: Explain why iron can be extracted with carbon but aluminium cannot.
topics.talk: Ask {him} why gold jewellery from ancient Greece still shines.

topics.title: Rates of reaction
topics.intro: Particles must collide with enough energy to react. More frequent or more energetic collisions mean a faster reaction: raise the temperature, concentration or surface area, or add a catalyst.
topics.teach: Explain, using collision theory, why powder reacts faster than lumps.
topics.talk: Drop a whole antacid tablet and a crushed one into water and compare.

topics.title: Exothermic and endothermic reactions
topics.intro: Exothermic reactions give out energy to the surroundings, so the temperature rises. Endothermic reactions take energy in, so the surroundings get colder.
topics.teach: Explain, in terms of bonds, why combustion is exothermic.
topics.talk: Look at how a reusable hand warmer works.

topics.title: Polymers, ceramics, composites and alloys
topics.intro: Materials are chosen for their properties. Polymers are long chains; ceramics are hard but brittle; composites combine two materials; alloys are mixtures of metals that are harder than the pure metal.
topics.teach: Explain why an alloy is harder than a pure metal, using a particle diagram.
topics.talk: Spot five composite materials at home or on a bike.

topics.title: Earth’s resources and recycling
topics.intro: Many resources are finite: once used, they are gone. Recycling, reusing and life-cycle assessments help us use them more wisely.
topics.teach: Explain why recycling aluminium saves so much energy.
topics.talk: Sort the recycling together and ask {him} which item saves the most energy to recycle.

topics.title: Motion graphs and terminal velocity
topics.intro: Distance–time graphs show speed as the gradient. Velocity–time graphs show acceleration as the gradient and distance as the area underneath. A falling object reaches terminal velocity when air resistance balances its weight.
topics.teach: Explain why a skydiver reaches a steady speed.
topics.talk: Drop a flat sheet of paper and a scrunched-up one together, and compare.

topics.title: Work, power and energy stores
topics.intro: Work is done when a force moves something: work done = force × distance. Lifting stores energy as gravitational potential energy; moving objects have kinetic energy.
topics.teach: Explain the energy transfers when a weightlifter lifts and drops a bar.
topics.talk: Ask {him} how much work {she} does climbing the stairs (weight × height).

topics.title: Heating and specific heat capacity
topics.intro: Energy moves from hot to cold by conduction, convection and radiation. Specific heat capacity tells you how much energy it takes to warm 1 kg of a material by 1 °C; water’s is very high.
topics.teach: Explain why the sea warms up more slowly than the sand in summer.
topics.talk: Feel a metal spoon and a wooden spoon from the same drawer: which feels colder, and why?

topics.title: Static electricity and electric fields
topics.intro: Rubbing two materials together can move electrons from one to the other, leaving both charged. Like charges repel, opposite charges attract, and a charged object is surrounded by an electric field.
topics.teach: Explain why a rubbed balloon sticks to a wall.
topics.talk: Rub a balloon on {her} hair and watch it lift.

topics.title: Refraction, lenses, colour and ultrasound
topics.intro: Light bends (refracts) when it changes speed between materials. Lenses use refraction to focus light; prisms split white light into a spectrum. Sound above 20 000 Hz is ultrasound, used for scans and sonar.
topics.teach: Explain why a straw looks bent in a glass of water.
topics.talk: Make a rainbow with a glass of water in sunlight.

topics.title: Stars, galaxies and the universe
topics.intro: Stars are born in clouds of dust and gas, shine by nuclear fusion, and die in different ways depending on their mass. Our Sun is one of hundreds of billions of stars in the Milky Way.
topics.teach: Explain how the life cycle of a massive star differs from the Sun’s.
topics.talk: Find Orion and Cassiopeia in the night sky, and tell each other their myths.

topics.title: Practical skills: methods, errors and evaluation
topics.intro: Good practical work means planning a fair test, taking repeat readings, spotting anomalies, calculating means and judging how far the evidence supports a conclusion.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between a random error and a systematic error.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to plan a fair test for which paper towel is most absorbent.

topics.title: Electrolysis
topics.intro: Electricity can split compounds that contain ions, if they are melted or dissolved so the ions can move. Positive ions go to the negative electrode; negative ions go to the positive electrode.
topics.teach: Explain why solid salt cannot be electrolysed but salt solution can.
topics.talk: Ask {him} how the aluminium in a drinks can was made.

topics.title: Electromagnetic induction
topics.intro: Moving a magnet in a coil of wire, or a wire in a magnetic field, induces a potential difference. Power stations, bike dynamos and wind turbines all use this.
topics.teach: Explain three ways to make a generator produce a bigger voltage.
topics.talk: Look at a wind turbine and talk about where its electricity comes from.

topics.title: Momentum
topics.intro: Momentum = mass × velocity. In a collision or explosion the total momentum is conserved. Spreading a collision over a longer time reduces the force: the idea behind crumple zones and airbags.
topics.teach: Explain why crumple zones make cars safer.
topics.talk: Ask {him} why you bend your knees when you land from a jump.

items.prompt: Using Kit’s results, explain how temperature affects the activity of amylase. Use the lock-and-key model in your answer. (6 marks)
hints: Describe the pattern: faster up to 37 °C, then slower, then none at 70 °C
Use figures from the table
Explain the rise: more kinetic energy, more collisions
Explain the fall: active site changes shape, enzyme denatured
Mention that the optimum is body temperature
items.model: As the temperature rises from 10 °C to 37 °C, the time for the starch to disappear falls from 300 s to 60 s, so the enzyme works faster. This is because the molecules have more kinetic energy, so starch collides with the active site more often. Above 37 °C the time rises again (150 s at 50 °C) and at 70 °C the starch never disappears. items.prompt: Is catching a falling ruler a reflex? Explain your answer, describing the path the nerve impulses take in Kit’s catch. (6 marks)
hints: It is NOT a reflex: it is a conscious response
The stimulus is detected by receptors in the eye
Sensory neurone to the brain, which decides

items.model: Catching the ruler is not a reflex, because Kit has to decide to catch it and she improves with practice. Light from the falling ruler is detected by receptors in her eyes. Impulses travel along sensory neurones to her brain, which processes the information and decides to respond. Impulses then travel along motor neurones to the effectors, the muscles in her hand, which contract. A true reflex, like pulling a hand off a hot pan, is automatic and goes through a relay neurone in the spinal cord without the conscious brain, so it is faster.

items.model: Water enters the root hair cells by osmosis and travels up the stem in the xylem to the leaves, where it evaporates and escapes through the stomata. items.model: The more reactive a metal is, the more strongly it holds on to other elements in its ore, so the harder it is to extract. Gold is so unreactive that it is found as the pure metal and just needs to be dug up. Iron is below carbon in the reactivity series, so heating iron oxide with carbon in a blast furnace removes the oxygen: carbon is more reactive and takes it. This is called reduction. Aluminium is above carbon, so carbon cannot take the oxygen away; it has to be extracted by electrolysis, which uses a lot of electricity. This explains why gold was used first, iron only once furnaces were hot enough, and aluminium only after 1886.

items.model: When she leaves the plane her weight is much bigger than the air resistance, so there is a resultant force downwards and she accelerates. items.prompt: Explain why a rubbed balloon becomes charged, and why it sticks to a wall even though the wall is not charged. (6 marks)
hints: Friction transfers electrons
The balloon gains electrons: negative
The jumper loses electrons: positive
Near the wall, the balloon repels electrons in the wall’s surface
The surface of the wall becomes slightly positive, so it attracts the balloon
items.model: When the balloon is rubbed on the jumper, friction transfers electrons from the jumper to the balloon. The balloon gains electrons, so it becomes negatively charged, and the jumper is left positively charged. When the negative balloon is held near the wall, it repels electrons in the surface of the wall, pushing them slightly away. This leaves the surface of the wall nearest the balloon with a small positive charge. Opposite charges attract, so the negative balloon is attracted to the positive surface and sticks to the wall, even though the wall as a whole has no overall charge.
